\subsection{Threats to Validity}
\label{sec:threats}

Four confounds limit causal attribution of the observed repo-level divergence.

\paragraph{Checkpoint selection.} Val-based selection is unavailable for runs with NaN validation loss (all \cwm{} repo-level runs, DeepSeek \cls{} s123), which default to the final epoch checkpoint. The Qwen3-8B \traj{} comparison (epoch 2: 72.92\% vs.\ epoch 3: 70.83\%) illustrates that a single epoch difference can shift accuracy by ${\sim}$2\pp{}. Val-selected and final-epoch checkpoints are not directly comparable; the magnitude of this confound is bounded by the epoch 2--3 gap observed within each formulation.

\paragraph{Evaluation sequence length.} \cwm{} accuracy varies by ${\sim}$9\pp{} across evaluation sequence lengths for the same checkpoint (seq2048: ${\sim}$65\% vs.\ seq4096: ${\sim}$56\%), driven by unparseable-rate differences that propagate through majority-class default assignment. \cls{} is invariant to this parameter. Cross-model \cwm{} comparisons use different eval lengths (Qwen3: 8192, DeepSeek: 4096) and are not directly comparable in absolute terms.

\paragraph{Preprocessing.} DeepSeek \cls{} accuracy ranges from 82.61\% (s42, drop preprocessing) to 74.93\% (s123, truncate preprocessing), a 7.68\pp{} spread that conflates preprocessing strategy, checkpoint selection method, and seed. The two strategies produce different effective training sets (67,343 vs.\ 70,748 samples) and different checkpoint selection regimes.

\paragraph{\traj{} training regime.} \traj{} uses a different training configuration: smaller training set (${\sim}$400 repo-level variants vs.\ ${\sim}$70K per-test instances), higher learning rate ($2{\times}10^{-4}$ vs.\ $5{\times}10^{-5}$), and variant-level labels. This asymmetry is inherent to the formulation (trajectory-level labels are only available at variant granularity), but precludes training-data-controlled comparison at repo level. The function-level downsample control (\S\ref{sec:repo}) partially addresses data volume but not label granularity.

\paragraph{Why does generation degrade at repo level?} The \cls{}--\cwm{} gap amplifies from 1--3\pp{} (function) to 19--26\pp{} (repo) because output space complexity increases nonlinearly. At function level, expected outputs are short strings (integers, booleans, short lists); at repo level, expected outputs are unconstrained test execution traces (mean ${\sim}$477 tokens). Autoregressive generation must produce token-exact matches across the full sequence, and errors compound multiplicatively. Constrained decoding could eliminate format failures, but parseable-only accuracy (38--43\%) remains well below majority baseline, indicating a deeper semantic gap.

\paragraph{Process vs.\ Outcome Supervision.}
Lightman et al.~\cite{lightman2023letsverify} and Uesato et al.~\cite{uesato2022solving} show process reward models (PRMs) outperform outcome reward models (ORMs) for mathematical reasoning; Math-Shepherd~\cite{wang2024mathshepherd} and OmegaPRM~\cite{luo2024omegaprm} scale process supervision via automated annotation. The PRM literature primarily compares supervision granularity given a fixed output format; our study additionally varies the output format itself (\cwm{} generation vs.\ \cls{} classification).
